Original fixtures check a MacPherson mechanism against closed-form lower-arm motion, upright orientation and telescoping length through compression/rebound/return sweeps. Further cases check steering with three preserved lengths and a top point on the upright axis, rigid-frame covariance, an analytic Jacobian against central differences with a noncoincident strut attachment, singular/collapsed/reversed axes, unreachable commands and failed-solve immutability. The source adapter rejects wrong types and each missing required point. The CLI fixture now checks both DWB and STRUT reports through the reader/adapter/solver, retaining unchanged source bytes. The existing DWB analytical and local-source checks pass after sharing the Newton iteration.

Local STRUT checks covered 81 cases on the front suspensions of BMW M3 E30, BMW 1M and BMW M3 E92: travel from -40 to +40 mm in 10 mm increments, each with -2/0/+2 mm source-X steering-anchor displacement. A separate Python calculation expanded the returned quaternions and directly checked three source distances, top-to-axis perpendicular error, positive axial length and extension. Maximum length errors were 2.532e-11, 2.878e-11 and 2.999e-11 m respectively; maximum perpendicular errors were 4.016e-12, 5.421e-12 and 3.164e-12 m. All cases converged within four updates. The earlier 81 DWB source cases were also rerun successfully. These are raw-design constraint checks, not measurements of original-game wheel motion, suspension forces or performance.

The current Windows ordinary Rust test total is 267; the eleven explicit GPU and six window tests retain their separate scope. Full source-frame/setup mapping, native wheel animation and original-game kinematics validation remain work ahead.

Suspension differential validation

Six original Rust kernel fixtures check closed-form parallel-wishbone and telescoping-strut velocities, all four differential columns against central pose differences, point-force torque and virtual power, ideal held force/moment balance and independently reconstructed rod/top reactions. Additional cases within these fixtures check rigid-frame rotation/translation covariance, mismatched/unconverged poses, invalid rates/points, excessive load amplification and map immutability. The CLI fixture covers both topologies, explicit rates/loads, report metadata and malformed/duplicate options with no partial JSON output. Together these added seven tests, bringing that milestone to 143 ordinary Windows tests; formatting and warning-free Clippy also pass.

Local source checks covered both axles of BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K at -30/0/+30 mm travel and +2 mm source-X rack displacement: 18 cases. Each used explicit synthetic rates [0.17, 0.025, -0.012, 0.009] m/s and a synthetic force [120, 2300, -300] N with torque [40, -15, 25] N m about the upright origin. An independent Python calculation compared velocities with solved poses at +/-0.001 seconds, expanded quaternions separately and reconstructed support moments from source anchors, rod directions and the ideal STRUT top reaction.

Across these cases the maximum origin-velocity difference was 6.787e-9 m/s and angular-velocity difference 8.047e-8 rad/s. Virtual-power discrepancy stayed below 1.288e-13 W, force-balance residual below 4.548e-13 N, and torque balance/reconstructed support/frame-moment errors below 5.685e-14 N m. These are numerical consistency results for raw source geometry and ideal massless supports under supplied loads. They do not validate original-game force transfer, tyre/spring laws, chassis dynamics or driving. Raw game/SDK records and temporary reports remain excluded from Git.

Spring linkage coupling validation

Five original Rust fixtures check DWB/STRUT spring length/rate and travel load against closed-form geometry, all four motion ratios and conservative loads against independently computed central length/energy differences, asymmetric damping passivity, point torque and virtual-power balance. They compare the same mount/law with the existing rigid-body spring sampler and verify rigid-frame rotation/translation covariance, direct frame reaction moments, invalid mounts/laws, coincidence/rate rejection and map immutability. An application fixture checks both topologies with and without damping, energy/power and held residuals, explicit metadata, and malformed/negative/duplicate options with no partial JSON output. The existing body-spring tests pass after sharing the scalar sampling path.

Local checks used both axles of BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K at -30/0/+30 mm travel with +2 mm source-X rack displacement: 18 cases. Rates were [0.17, 0.025, -0.012, 0.009] m/s. The explicitly synthetic spring used fixed anchor [0, 0.6, 0] m, upright-local attachment [0.07, -0.08, 0.1] m, rest length 0.65 m, stiffness 12000 N/m, compression slopes 80/20 N s/m with knee 0.05 m/s and rebound slopes 140/30 N s/m with knee 0.07 m/s. These mounts and parameters were not taken from or calibrated to Assetto Corsa.

An independent Python quaternion/length calculation agreed within 1.111e-16 m; its +/-0.001 s central length-rate differences agreed within 5.922e-9 m/s. Maximum power-balance discrepancy was 1.843e-14 W, held force residual 5.685e-13 N and held moment residual 2.132e-14 N m. That spring-coupling milestone reached 149 ordinary Windows Rust tests, with the eleven explicit GPU and five window tests separate. These checks establish a coupled geometric spring element, not source force parity, constrained dynamics, car equilibrium or a native driving session.

Fixed-frame suspension dynamics validation

Seven original Rust fixtures cover analytical DWB/STRUT accelerations, all travel/rack acceleration inputs and local-point centripetal acceleration against independent central pose/quaternion differences, invalid rates/accelerations, and circular free-motion dynamics. The circular fixture checks effective mass, inertial bias, centripetal reactions, a closed-form trajectory and second-order time-step convergence; final travel/rate errors are each below 2e-8 in metres and m/s respectively. Additional cases check off-axis COM/full non-diagonal tensors, gravity, Newton/Euler force and moment balance, the Lagrangian identity b = 0.5*M'(h)*hdot^2, damped energy, exact local constraints, fixed-frame covariance and failed-final-stage rollback. The damped fixtures run 1000 steps at 0.5 ms for both topologies and reduce energy below 40% of its initial value within their numerical tolerance.

Two CLI fixtures exercise both source topologies through a complete 250-step run, verify changing travel, recorded times, energy loss and near-zero travel holding residual, and preserve original fixture source bytes. Rejection cases cover schema/version/unknown/missing fields, invalid mass/tensor, byte/step/record/spring limits, bad duration and a run whose final integration stage leaves the local domain. Errors print no partial JSON. Those nine additions brought the fixed-frame milestone to 158 ordinary Windows Rust tests; the eleven explicit GPU and six window tests retain their separate scope.

Local checks ran both axles of BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K with the published synthetic JSON: 1500 total 1-ms steps, covering 0.25 s per mechanism. A separate Python calculation expanded the returned quaternions and independently rechecked 156 recorded states against original raw hardpoint distances/top-axis geometry and Newton/Euler force/moment balance, including rotated full inertia and COM lever arms. Maximum distance error was 6.734e-11 m, STRUT perpendicular error 1.163e-11 m, auxiliary travel residual 9.759e-14 N, force residual 2.701e-13 N and moment residual 2.043e-14 N m. Recorded spring/kinetic energy decreased in all six runs.

These results establish an independently implemented massive upright on fixed massless supports under explicit synthetic inputs. They do not establish original-game unsprung dynamics, source mass/preload/spring mapping, a moving chassis, tyre/contact forces or driving. Local source files and raw workbench reports remain excluded from Git. See the equations and integration contract.

Coupled chassis dynamics validation

The normalized mass solver has an original fixture spanning mixed coordinate scales and active dimensions 7..10, with asymmetric/negative/nonfinite/singular rejection. Seven further original fixtures check two-mass spring recoil against analytical initial accelerations, whole-system momentum/COM behavior, four-corner analytical free fall, a spinning/translating chassis with independent global Newton/Euler balance, mechanical energy derivative versus external power minus dissipation, world rotation/translation covariance, second-order time-step convergence, bad topology/load counts, ill-conditioned mass ratios and failed-last-corner rollback. Both DWB and STRUT are exercised; full non-diagonal COM tensors and moving-frame Coriolis/centrifugal terms are included.

Two application fixtures run a four-corner source configuration through the CLI, verify actual chassis recoil, energy loss, small momentum drift, explicit frame/mass metadata, relative-path resolution and unchanged source bytes. Rejection covers strict schema/version/unknown/missing fields, byte/corner/record/step limits, bad mounting quaternion/data selection and a run that leaves the local domain on its last corner. The shared spring parser remains covered by the earlier fixed-frame fixtures. That coupled-chassis milestone reached 168 ordinary Windows Rust tests; eleven explicit offscreen GPU and five native-window tests retain their separate scope.

Local coupled checks used BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K geometry with the published synthetic four-corner mounts, masses/tensors and springs, zero gravity and zero external loads. Each was run for 0.25 s at 1 ms and 0.5 ms: six runs and 2250 total steps. An independent Python quaternion/inertia calculation rechecked 624 recorded upright states for source/world COM composition, body Newton/Euler balance, chassis recoil balance and total linear/orbital-plus-spin angular momentum reporting. Maximum force residual was 1.645e-12 N, moment residual 1.939e-12 N m and auxiliary travel residual 7.750e-13 N. World COM composition agreed within 8.882e-16 m; independently recomputed momentum components agreed within 4.264e-14 in their units.

The explicit integrator has measurable finite-step drift. Across the three 1-ms runs, maximum total linear-momentum drift was 1.804e-4 kg m/s, angular-momentum drift 2.028e-4 kg m^2/s and total-COM drift 2.155e-8 m. At 0.5 ms the maxima were 4.526e-5 kg m/s, 5.085e-5 kg m^2/s and 5.359e-9 m respectively. Every car's drift decreased by a factor above 3.7 when the step halved, consistent with the original second-order convergence fixtures. Recorded mechanical energy decreased under damping in all six runs; this is not a universal stability or conservation guarantee.

These tests establish coupled native rigid-body/support behavior under explicit synthetic inputs. Source mounting, right/left conventions, masses/preload, original handling, wheel spin, road/tyre contact and rendered driving remain unvalidated or incomplete. No original content or local run dumps are published. See the coupled equations.

Axisymmetric wheel dynamics validation

Seven new original Rust fixtures cover wheel mass/tensor/axle/state bounds, duplicate attachment and ignored-load rejection, analytical internal motor recoil versus external axle torque, a 0.5-s coaxial motor trajectory and motor work, four-rotor global Newton/Euler balance with external wheel forces/torques, gyroscopic/drive power versus an independent central energy derivative, world covariance, second-order convergence and failed-final-spin rollback. Tilted axles and phase values through the angle bound verify axisymmetric inertia and momentum independently of visual phase. Both DWB and STRUT are included. The normalized matrix fixture now spans 7..14 coordinates; prior wheel-less fixtures still pass.

Two CLI fixtures check four additional wheel masses/spin DOFs, actual angle/rate evolution, opposite motor reactions and near-zero spin residual, and reject invalid axes, nonphysical inertia, bad state ranges, missing/unknown wheel fields without partial JSON. Those nine additions brought the wheel milestone to 177 ordinary Windows Rust tests. The eleven explicit GPU and five native-window tests remain separate; no wheel animation or contact behavior is implied.

Local checks used BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K raw geometry with chassis-wheels.json's synthetic mass split, inertias, frames, springs and +/-8 N m internal motors. Each ran 0.25 s at 1 ms and 0.5 ms: six runs, 2250 total steps and 6024 recorded wheel/upright pairs. An independent Python quaternion/inertia calculation rechecked wheel/world COM composition, rotor spin balance, bearing/motor transfer, upright/chassis Newton/Euler balance and system orbital-plus-spin momentum. Maximum force residual was 2.157e-12 N, moment residual 2.486e-12 N m, spin residual 3.376e-14 N m and auxiliary travel residual 1.134e-12 N. COM composition agreed within 8.882e-16 m and independently recomputed momentum components within 5.685e-14 in their units.

Across the 1-ms runs, maximum linear-momentum drift was 8.932e-5 kg m/s, angular-momentum drift 1.072e-4 kg m^2/s and total-COM drift 1.065e-8 m. At 0.5 ms the maxima were 2.241e-5 kg m/s, 2.687e-5 kg m^2/s and 2.648e-9 m. Every car's drift decreased by a factor above 3.7 when the step halved. Motor work was computed from constant torque times relative angle change; trapezoidal dissipation sampled every 1 ms left a combined integration/quadrature energy residual below 1.243e-3 J at 1-ms steps and 3.631e-4 J at 0.5-ms steps. Energy can increase under motor work, as seen for Ferrari; this is consistent with damping still dissipating energy.

This establishes explicit coupled wheel rotors and actuator reaction under synthetic inputs. It does not validate AC unsprung/wheel mass partition, axle/side conventions, gearbox/CV-shaft torque paths, tyres, brakes, road traction or rendered driving. No local game data or run dumps are published. See rotor equations and load conventions.

Normal contact and force-stage validation

Four original normal-law fixtures check the analytical flat load, separation/first-touch behavior, zero-attraction damping clamp and mechanical power balance. Cambered-circle geometry checks support height, moment, zero normal spin damping/axle torque; independent central geometric/energy differences check gap velocity and elastic wrench. World covariance, axial degeneracy, excessive penetration and invalid law/plane bounds are also covered.

Three coupled fixtures verify force-independent snapshots against dynamic body states, bit-identical constant-provider versus constant-load stepping, actual provider offsets/state-dependent force evaluation, and rollback for failures at each of the three stages. A full four-corner fixture checks analytical static equilibrium: 300 kg chassis, four 35 kg uprights and four 20 kg wheels, gravity 9.81 m/s^2, 200000 N/m normal stiffness and 20000 N/m suspension springs. Its equilibrium wheel/chassis height is 0.2936235 m, each normal load is 1275.3 N and explicit spring rest length is 0.6367875 m. A 3-mm height perturbation adds 3.6 J; 1000 steps at 1 ms reduce excess energy below 1% and return height within 5e-5 m in this damped fixture.

The force-stage fixture also checks initialization under balanced large preload: force-aware construction accepts a valid balanced state whose artificial unloaded acceleration would violate the numeric limit. Matrix/body validation remains active in both construction paths.

Two CLI fixtures check normal support with gravity, contact energy/dissipation reporting and changing loads, and reject missing/unused planes, bad laws/normals, unknown fields and excessive intermediate-stage penetration without partial JSON. These nine additions brought the ordinary Windows Rust total to 186 before the finite-face additions below. Eleven explicit GPU and six native-window tests remain separate; no rendered contact or track collision is implied.

Local raw-geometry checks used BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K with the published synthetic plane benchmark at 1-ms and 0.5-ms steps for one second each: six runs, 9000 steps and 4824 recorded contacts. An independent Python circle/inertia calculation rechecked gap, load, torque, damping power and whole-system Newton/Euler balance including gravity and plane forces. Maximum geometric difference was 1.111e-16 m, normal-force difference 2.274e-11 N, contact-moment difference 1.883e-13 N m and damping-power difference 7.106e-15 W. Global force/moment residuals stayed below 4.505e-11 N and 6.600e-11 N m. Maximum observed penetration was 0.014731 m, below the explicit 0.08 m limit.

Total mechanical energy including normal compliance decreased in all six runs. Sampled 5-ms trapezoidal dissipation left a combined integration/quadrature residual below 0.018352 J at 1-ms integration and 0.005865 J at 0.5 ms. Final chassis heights differed by less than 6.3e-8 m between those steps. At one second the normal loads were within 0.92% of total weight but still evolving; these are transient checks, not a static source calibration. Normal parameters, initial height, frame/mass assignment and preload remain synthetic. There is no track triangle, tyre width, tangential force, CCD or original-game comparison in this benchmark.

Reproducible examples

Tests use small original fixtures generated in temporary directories, including complete original KN5 structures and explicitly header-only fixtures for the lightweight inspector. Do not add copied cars, tracks, textures, audio, or SDK archives to the repository. A parser change should include a minimal example proving the new behavior and invalid input that must be diagnosed.

Finite track-face contact validation

Six additional ordinary Rust fixtures cover finite face queries, both windings, slope/edge/plane clipping, metadata, invalid bounds and the exact 4096/4097 candidate-cap boundary; finite support, airborne/missing support, shared seams, overhead decks, backside overlap, excessive penetration, cambered slope load/moment and minimum-normal filtering; and CLI plane/track equivalence, explicit spawn placement, face provenance and invalid/ambiguous configuration rejection without partial JSON. The current ordinary Windows Rust total is 267; eleven explicit GPU and six window tests retain their separate scope.

The local synthetic BMW geometry benchmark on Drift loaded system surface defaults before the selected track definitions, retaining 54522 support triangles. With AC_PIT_0, explicit COM offset [0,-0.264,0], a 0.5-ms step and one-second duration, every recorded wheel selected 01ROAD; maximum penetration was 0.014618 m, below the 0.08 m bound. Omitting system defaults initially omitted that road key and produced airborne wheels; this is why the published example supplies both surface files. Loader and duplicate-marker diagnostics remain visible.

This proves finite-face normal support on this local geometry with synthetic masses, mounts and force parameters. It does not prove edge/vertex collision, CCD, friction/traction, rendered native driving or original AC calibration. Crossing unsmoothed face boundaries can change the law discontinuously; analytical plane energy tests do not establish energy continuity for arbitrary meshes.

Independent Python reloading of the installed physical triangles checked selected source indices/meshes, finite barycentric inclusion, upward normals, circle support geometry, force/moment and dissipation for two one-second BMW runs at 1-ms and 0.5-ms steps (3000 steps, 1608 saved contacts). Geometry differed by at most 1.111e-16 m, normal load by 2.229e-11 N, contact torque by 9.060e-14 N m and damping power by 2.843e-14 W. Whole-system Newton/Euler residuals were below 5.700e-11 N and 1.047e-8 N m, respectively, including the large world-origin moment arm. At the denser 5-ms record cadence, maximum recorded penetration was 0.014661 m. The sampled energy/dissipation quadrature residual decreased from 0.013680 J to 0.004361 J; final chassis heights differed by 5.910e-8 m. These are local numerical consistency checks, not original-game comparisons.

Tangential contact validation

Seven additional ordinary Rust fixtures cover forward/reverse spinning-wheel traction and axle reaction, force-free pure rolling, unsaturated and saturated combined slip in all sign combinations, ellipse limits, dissipative mechanical power, cambered material-point torque, world covariance, airborne/separating/no-grip cases, disabled directions and invalid coefficients/scales. A coupled four-wheel fixture checks motor-driven chassis momentum and work minus normal/suspension/slip losses, with decreasing quadrature/integration residual at halved step. Session and CLI fixtures check selected-surface scaling, missing finite faces, traction, loss aggregation and malformed/missing parameters without partial JSON. The ordinary Windows Rust total is 267; eleven explicit GPU and six window tests remain separate.

The local synthetic BMW/Drift example ran for one second with rear torques +100/-100 N m and all-wheel friction. At a 0.5-ms step the chassis moved about 0.277 m horizontally and reached about 0.556 m/s horizontal speed through contact traction. This is not a controller, calibrated acceleration measurement or original drivetrain simulation. A separate 1-ms run supplied step comparison. Independent Python reloading of source triangles checked normal geometry, material slip, ellipse forces/torques/dissipation and complete world Newton/Euler balance over 1608 saved contacts. Global force residual stayed below 4.429e-11 N and world-origin moment residual below 8.198e-9 N m. At the denser 5-ms record cadence, maximum recorded penetration was 0.014728 m. Sampled motor-work/energy/dissipation residuals were 0.014229 J and 0.025071 J respectively; this coarse output quadrature does not establish convergence. Full-step analytical-fixture quadrature supplies the convergence test. The explicit finite-face, no-CCD and synthetic-parameter limitations still apply.

Scheduled brake validation

Seven additional ordinary Rust fixtures cover brake torque symmetry, bounds, continuity at transition rates, zero input/rest, passivity and invalid parameters; transactional internal-load changes; and an analytical two-rotor brake solution for both DWB/STRUT mounts and spin signs. The analytical fixture checks opposing upright recoil, angular momentum, kinetic energy, no sign crossing at tested steps and second-order convergence. Two timeline fixtures check interpolation, endpoint holding, time/input bounds, ordering and counts. Two CLI fixtures check a scheduled accelerate/brake sequence, net torque and power/loss reporting, deceleration, malformed inputs without partial JSON, and airborne braking with no road provider. The ordinary Windows Rust total is 267; explicit GPU/window test scopes remain unchanged.

The local synthetic BMW/Drift four-second sequence reached about 0.61448 m/s before brake application, then fell to 0.11753 m/s at two seconds and 0.001056 m/s at four seconds with the 0.5-ms step. This residual speed is expected for the regularized law; it is not a static wheel-lock or exact stopping-distance validation. All source-frame, contact and original-game calibration limitations remain.

Independent Python checks reloaded Drift's physical triangles and re-evaluated scheduled drive/brake inputs, regularized torque and power, finite support, tangential slip forces and whole-system Newton/Euler balance for four-second runs at 1-ms and 0.5-ms steps (12000 steps, 1608 saved wheel contacts). Brake torque/power matched the independent formula at saved states; maximum global force/moment residuals were below 1e-7 N and 1e-7 N m. Contact penetration remained below 0.014728 m. The coarse 20-ms output quadrature left motor-work/energy/dissipation residuals of 0.369482 J and 0.358923 J; this sampling does not establish convergence of the full-run energy budget. The analytical rotor fixture supplies a separate full-step convergence check. Original-game brake validation remains outstanding.

Prescribed rack validation

Six additional ordinary Rust fixtures cover moving-rack geometry/velocities, upright/wheel angular motion, actuator work and whole-system momentum derivatives against independent central state differences; actual stage ordering, final-state commit, continuity guards and rollback on rack/force failure at every stage, invalid final slot counts and invalid diagnostic prescriptions; step-halving work convergence, internal momentum conservation and fixed-prescription equivalence; Hermite analytical derivatives, velocity continuity, endpoint hold, domains and interior cubic overshoot; and a contact-supported CLI turn, power aggregation and malformed profiles without partial JSON. The ordinary Windows Rust total is 267; eleven explicit GPU and six window tests retain their separate scope.

The three-second local synthetic BMW/Drift run turned with two prescribed front racks, rear motor drive and scheduled braking. At 1.8 seconds its world yaw rate was about 0.03089 rad/s. Maximum recorded actuator force component was about 779.2 N; the drive both supplied and recovered energy during the path. These are outcomes of explicit synthetic parameters, not measured original steering or FFB behavior. Both 1-ms and 0.5-ms runs were checked against independently reloaded local source hardpoints and physical road triangles, including DWB lengths, STRUT lengths/coaxiality, travel and steering-anchor offsets. Source constraint residuals stayed within 1e-10 m; source files were not modified or published. Full validation numbers and timestep limits below describe this local workbench only.

Across the two local three-second runs (9000 steps, 1608 saved contacts), independent Hermite evaluation differed from reported rack derivatives by at most 1.249e-16 in their respective units; rack power differed by at most 3.276e-14 W. Source distance/coaxial/travel residuals stayed below 9.973e-11 m. Global Newton/Euler force/moment residuals were below 3.562e-11 N and 6.683e-9 N m, and maximum recorded normal penetration was 0.014971 m. Net sampled rack work was about 1.51345 J. The 15-ms output quadrature left combined input-work/energy/loss residuals of 0.309448 J and 0.320561 J; it does not prove full-run energy convergence. The separate full-step synthetic fixture checks convergence. No original-game telemetry, steering-wheel/FFB mapping or rendered driving is established by these checks.

Native driving window validation

Five additional ordinary CPU fixtures cover held-key release, brake-key aliases, cleared commands/autorepeat, forward/reverse input, smooth rate/acceleration-limited steering, live override of offline schedules, coupled acceleration/steering/braking/reset, invalid command atomicity and translated-camera projection. A sixth explicit window fixture uses wholly original car/track geometry/configuration, runs 2.4 seconds through the shared native key handler, and checks 121 presentations, four readbacks, two roots, acceleration/yaw, braking and changed pixels at a fixed camera. Ordinary Windows Rust total is 267; eleven explicit offscreen GPU tests and six window tests have separate scope. The diagnostic key handler is verified; independent physical keyboard operation is not established.

The local optimized BMW M3 E30/Drift diagnostic executed 4800 physics ticks at 2000 Hz and 121 presented frames with readbacks at 0, 1, 1.6 and 2.4 seconds. Horizontal chassis speed reached about 0.8903 m/s at 1.6 seconds and fell to about 0.1374 m/s after braking at 2.4 seconds. World yaw rate at 1.6 seconds was about 0.02712 rad/s. The car root moved about one metre, with changed native surface pixels and unchanged camera. Selected initial/turn captures are published as progress illustrations. Those initial captures predate the explicit subtree animation described below; glass/lighting remain approximate.

Two optimized diagnostics measured about 0.881 and 0.939 seconds inside the physics-clock advances for 2.4 simulated seconds on this local Windows/RTX 2080 machine. This is a local headroom measurement, not a cross-hardware frame-rate guarantee; rendering, loading and platform input have separate costs. Debug builds can fall behind and pause through the explicit lag guard. Body/wall response, edge/vertex contact, CCD, static stiction, original vehicle calibration and remaining gameplay systems are not established by this milestone.

Native articulation validation

Three additional ordinary fixtures bring the Rust total to 220. The KN5 fixture checks nested subtree draw ranges, parent/world transforms, inactive empty ranges, identical ordinary geometry and truncation rejection; node-only loading still has empty ranges. The application fixtures check complete disjoint draw partitioning, preserved rest placement, physical travel and spin about the source visual pivot with a translated/rotated chassis, and upright separation from rotor spin. Missing/ambiguous/inactive/empty/overlapping bindings, nonexistent slots/wheels, unknown fields/kinds and the 16-binding cap are rejected.

The existing explicit native-drive window test now generates eight original wheel/upright subtrees. It runs the same diagnostic twice, with articulation enabled and disabled, and checks ten versus two GPU roots, identical initial pixels and chassis state, different driven-frame pixels, and divergent spinning-wheel/nonspinning-upright transforms. Eleven explicit offscreen GPU tests and six desktop-window tests retain their separate scope. This verifies persistent group transforms and rendered effects without requiring installed game files; physical keyboard/device and original-game behavior remain unverified.

The local BMW M3 E30 example explicitly selects four WHEEL_* and four SUSP_* nodes from the user's installed near-LOD model. No model, original texture, hardpoint or node-coordinate dataset is distributed as a fixture. Source pivot mapping preserves the model's original rest placement, while synthetic physical mount dimensions still require calibration before visual tyre alignment or original suspension behavior can be claimed.

The local optimized BMW/Drift articulation diagnostic completed 4800 physics ticks, 121 native presentations and four readbacks over 2.4 simulated seconds with 13 persistent roots. At the 1.6-second capture, the eight selected groups plus the shared chassis pose gave nine distinct root transforms. The selected flattened image is published in the site gallery. This is visual integration evidence, not validation against an original-game live run.

Source wheel geometry validation

Three additional ordinary application fixtures bring the Rust test total to 223. They cover all four corners with a rotated/translated chassis, nonzero initial DWB/STRUT travel, nonzero wheel-centre levers, explicit opposite-side frame rotations, alternate compounds and retained source provenance. Initial world centres match independently computed source-footprint positions within 1e-10 m, and source files are unchanged by loading.

The contact fixture checks the radius actually used by the force law: a source radius and 5-mm compression produce 1000 N at 200000 N/m with zero initial velocity. Editing the original fixture radius adds 20 mm compression and raises force to 5000 N on reload. Editing fixture track changes the registered centre; the loader does not retain stale source dimensions. Error cases cover both/neither frame choices, mismatched/unknown/duplicate corners, missing wheels, bad compounds/unknown fields, duplicate explicit/source radius choices and missing explicit radii. Eleven explicit offscreen GPU and six native-window fixtures retain separate scope.

The local BMW/Drift source-geometry run completed both the three-second offline workbench (201 records) and a 2.4-second native diagnostic (121 presentations, four readbacks, 13 roots). An independent script reloaded the typed car report and checked initial world centres against source offsets composed with the reported chassis quaternion; maximum difference was 7.106e-15 m. All four selected normal radii matched the tyre reader. This establishes registration to the current source-coordinate interpretation, not original-game setup correctness.

Corrected source-model pivot differences from physical rest centres remained approximately 0.011418 m at the front and 0.019575 m at the rear, and are exposed in native metadata. Source dimensions replaced the previous synthetic footprint and 0.3-m radii, while explicit source-frame rotations, masses and force parameters remain synthetic. Native diagnostic horizontal speed was about 0.87854 m/s at 1.6 s and 0.14030 m/s after braking at 2.4 s; yaw rate at 1.6 s was about 0.02517 rad/s. The selected native capture is a progress illustration; original-game parity, equilibrium, source spring/mass/drivetrain mapping and full body collision remain unverified or incomplete.

Source reflection validation

Three additional ordinary fixtures bring the Rust total to 226. Session checks use asymmetric original DWB/STRUT geometry at multiple travel/rack values. They verify reflected positions and point transforms, proper orientation conjugation, polar linear/point velocity and acceleration, axial angular velocity/acceleration, generalized loads, constraint force/moment reactions and invariant virtual work. Existing source-type/missing-point validation is preserved.

A coupled application fixture compares original and explicitly reflected source corners for both topologies over 50 physical ticks each. It includes a moving/rotating chassis, spring recoil, normal/tangential road contact, prescribed steering, internal motor and brake torque. Reflected linear/angular momentum, chassis/wheel states, kinetic energy, normal force and slip dissipation agree within the fixture tolerances. The same signed +X rotor input is used in each reflected assembly, consistent with axial-vector transformation. Eleven explicit offscreen GPU and six native-window tests retain their separate scope.

On local BMW, an independent check reloaded the raw suspension report, applied only each configured hardpoint-X reflection and checked all 201 records of the three-second offline drive. Maximum rod-length error was 9.927e-11 m, maximum STRUT coaxial distance error 8.679e-11 m and travel error zero at report precision. At the reference pose all selected chassis anchors point inward relative to their source corner; both source mounting frames retain +Y up and +Z forward. These are source-geometry/solver checks, not an original-game kinematics comparison.

The updated BMW/Drift native diagnostic completed 121 presentations and four readbacks over 2.4 simulated seconds with 13 persistent roots. Horizontal speed at 1.6 s was about 0.87863 m/s and fell to 0.14108 m/s after braking at 2.4 s; yaw rate at 1.6 s was about 0.02576 rad/s. The gallery's latest source-dimensions capture has been refreshed from this run. The earlier source-registration measurements above describe the prior frame choice. Source setup/camber/toe, tyre/drivetrain laws, mass/inertia/preload and original handling parity remain unvalidated.

Coupled impulse validation

Five additional ordinary fixtures bring the Rust total to 231. Analytical DWB/STRUT cases with/without rotors distinguish free vertical travel from horizontally carried mass. A 30 N s vertical chassis impulse changes a 300-kg chassis speed by 0.1 m/s while free upright/rotor centres remain at rest; kinetic energy increases by 1.5 J. Horizontal response includes the 35-kg upright and optional 20-kg rotor.

A full 14-DOF fixture with rotated/translating chassis, travel/spin and fixed/moving racks checks external global momentum jumps, exact retained poses/angles/rack state, point-response prediction and kinetic/external/rack work balance. Another compares the impulse operator with loaded-minus-baseline instantaneous force response at a nonzero rotating, spinning, moving-rack state, checking all free rates without acceleration bias. Fixed-rack restitution cases e = 0, 0.3 and 1 check separating speed and analytical passive energy loss. Invalid inputs/directions, numeric/rate bound failures and exact zero-impulse behavior are covered transactionally.

Windows/Linux CI also executes the original coupled_impulse example. Its off-centre e = 0.4 fixture has inverse effective mass about 0.0031550912 1/kg, external work -532.472718 J and energy residual -2.274e-13 J on the local run. These are numerical fixture outcomes, not crash measurements. Eleven offscreen GPU and six window tests retain separate scope. No new native body collision or screenshot is claimed: geometry features, contact generation, CCD, friction and simultaneous contacts still need integration and validation.

Native WALL geometry validation

Ten additional ordinary fixtures bring the Rust total to 267. Six ground fixtures cover finite double-sided wall patches, margin/no-contact cases, AABB false positives rejected by edge-axis SAT, vertex touching, winding invariance, full pitch/roll/world covariance, invalid inputs/degenerate triangles, hidden physical WALL selection, source provenance and separation from road support. They exercise the 4096/4097 candidate boundary, height-aware filtering with 4097 separated triangles and rejection of 250001 input wall triangles. Existing finite support queries retain their contracts through the shared spatial helper.

Two session fixtures independently reconstruct collider bounds through graphics/model/world mappings, ignore an unreferenced outlier and preserve source bytes. Invalid mappings, flat/hidden/skinned geometry and oversized input are rejected. Two CLI fixtures verify source spawn composition, contact provenance and a rolled pose; malformed/oversized requests, missing markers, report overflow after an earlier successful probe and unknown fields print no partial JSON. Eleven offscreen GPU and six desktop-window tests keep their separate scope.

Local Drift supplies 2546 retained WALL triangles across eight meshes. The BMW proxy uses the 106 supported collider triangles (318 indexed references); its half extents are about [0.858949, 0.632198, 2.182051] m after the documented mapping. The example's three poses report 0, 4 and 4 triangle contacts. These are static geometry probes, including intentional overlaps, not playable collision outcomes.

An independent Python check reloads raw source geometry and checks 80 poses, including pitch/roll, using a world-space SAT implementation against the native box-local implementation. All contact sets match: 66 triangle contacts and 268 clipped points. Separation differs by at most 1.555e-15 m; point-to-source-plane error is below 1.477e-14 m, with expanded-box excess about 1.001e-9 m from the explicit clipping tolerance. Barycentric finite-triangle inclusion is also checked. The collider bounds agree with the independent source reader. Original files remain local; no reusable game geometry is published as a fixture.

This verifies the bounded WALL geometry subset. It does not validate the original convex collider, all obstacle classes, TOI/CCD, collision response/nonpenetration or original-game handling. Native driving remains unconnected to these patches until the coupled manifold solver is implemented.

Simultaneous contact validation

The simultaneous-contact milestone added seven ordinary Rust fixtures (248 total at that stage); eleven explicit offscreen GPU and six window tests keep their separate scope. Five core fixtures cover analytical free-suspension sticking/sliding, anisotropic oblique friction versus independently applied alternative impulses, rotated/translated response, 64 redundant points, global momentum and energy balance with fixed/moving racks, exact empty/separating no-ops and rollback on invalid input or nonconvergence. Application fixtures connect wholly original generated collider/WALL/road geometry to a coupled impact, verify fixed positions and energy loss, and exercise matching point/normal deduplication and the exact 64/65 point boundary. All run without a game installation or display. Existing point-impulse and continuous-force fixtures still pass through the shared factorization and impulse application.

The local BMW M3 E30/Drift diagnostic on 2026-10-24 used examples/wall-impact.json and examples/chassis-wall-impact.json, synthetic mass/force parameters, identity model mapping, AC_PIT_0 offset [-5.5, -0.04, 0] m, world velocity [-3, 0, -2] m/s and friction 0.3. Four source triangle patches produced 14 retained points. The explicit 1024-sweep/1e-4 m/s settings converged at sweep 533 with projected residual 9.997e-5 m/s. Kinetic energy changed from 7410 to 187.425925 J; external contact work was -7222.574075 J, rack work zero and energy-balance residual -1.819e-12 J. The independent momentum audit found linear and angular residuals below 6.5e-13 kg m/s and 3.5e-10 kg m^2/s respectively. Source diagnostics remain visible, including the unrelated duplicate Drift start slot.

An independent report audit reconstructs total linear/angular momenta, per-point normal/tangent decomposition, friction cones, normal complementarity, sliding direction, aggregate impulse/moment and unchanged positions/angles. Raw source geometry/reports remain local. Stricter 1e-7 m/s solves of these nearly parallel facets did not converge within 1024 sweeps and were correctly rejected. These results validate this bounded fixed-pose synthetic impact only: no rendered collision, original-game comparison, overlap repair, bounce, TOI or continuous native driving response is established.

Prescribed sweep validation

The prescribed-sweep milestone added six ordinary Rust fixtures (254 total at that stage). Four ground fixtures check an analytical wall crossing with clear endpoints, exact endpoint and initial-overlap cases, stationary/separating paths, pure rotation with clear endpoints, an offset collider rotating about a separate reference, analytical first-proximity fractions, quaternion sign invariance, rotated/translated world covariance and finite-face rejection of an infinite-plane false positive. Invalid poses/settings, the exact 4096/4097 swept candidate boundary and an exhausted iteration budget fail explicitly. Two CLI fixtures check source-spawn rebasing, retained patches/provenance, unchanged files, malformed/oversized inputs, later-record failure without partial stdout and the 4096 total-contact report cap. No game files or display are needed for these tests; the eleven offscreen GPU and six window tests remain separate.

Local BMW M3 E30/Drift validation on 2026-10-25 used wall-sweep examples/wall-sweep.json, the same explicit collider mapping as the static queries and a 1e-6 m proximity tolerance. Translation from AC_PIT_0 offset [0,-0.04,0] to [-8,-0.04,0] reported fraction 0.6827891160 in 3 evaluations, with 8 candidates and 2 patches. A pi-radian yaw at reference offset [-4,-0.04,0] reported fraction 0.2811107425 in 58 evaluations, with 6 candidates and 1 patch despite clear endpoint poses. The clear path toward local Z=-2 used 4 candidates and 2 evaluations.

An independent Python audit reads raw local WALL geometry and computes SAT in world space. Its swept candidate sets agree with the native report; 1001 sampled poses per path (3003 total) agree with the reported crossing/clear classification. At the two returned events the independently computed minimum gaps were 9.9999999e-7 and 1.0009540e-6 m. Poses 1e-4 fraction before each event are separated; poses 1e-4 after overlap. The clear path's minimum sampled SAT gap was 3.813879 m. Sampling supports these specific traces; the analytical fixtures and conservative speed bound establish the algorithm's scope. It is not original-game parity, a guarantee for arbitrary integrated force trajectories, or rendered native collision response. Research reports and source geometry remain local.

First WALL event validation

The first-event milestone added six ordinary fixtures (260 total at that stage). Three physics fixtures verify selected fractions 0, 1e-8, 0.2, 0.7 and 1 against the retained translation/rotation proposal; exact full-step equivalence and zero-time state; moving-rack callback offsets and selected prescriptions; rollback for selector errors, invalid fractions and failed final rack/force callbacks; and an analytical free translation stopped at a plane, impulsed, then advanced for the remaining time. Three session fixtures connect original generated collider/WALL geometry to that operator, verify source provenance and unchanged impact pose, elapsed/remaining accounting, clear-path equivalence, initial proximity returning zero time, and rollback of the entire segment on sweep/contact/parameter failure. The existing application fixture additionally checks a moving source-wall event with friction disabled to isolate integration. All use original literals without game files or display. The eleven offscreen GPU and six window tests retain separate scope.

On 2026-10-26, wall-step examples/wall-step.json used the local BMW M3 E30/Drift, synthetic mechanics, AC_PIT_0 offset [-5.45,-0.04,0] m, initial world velocity [-3,0,-2] m/s, friction 0.3 and a 0.01-second proposal. First proximity occurred at fraction 0.3775199161, consuming 0.00377519916 s and returning 0.00622480084 s. Two triangle patches supplied two contact points. Pre-impact kinetic energy was 7389.628678 J; impact work was -2432.747145 J and post-impact energy 4956.881532 J. The impact energy-balance residual was -4.55e-13 J. Independent aggregate momentum checks gave linear/angular residuals below 1.3e-12 kg m/s and 2.1e-10 kg m^2/s; interpolation, unchanged impact pose and total duration agree. A static geometry re-query at the committed event pose matches both reported source patches.

At the first-event milestone the example explicitly used 1e-4 m/s contact tolerance. A synthetic first-contact fixture with friction 0.3 failed to converge at 1e-7 m/s within 1024 sweeps (residual about 2.149e-4 m/s), and was rejected. The integration fixture therefore verifies the geometry/motion bridge with zero friction; separate analytical fixtures retain friction validation. This exposed a convergence limitation; the subsequent normal-projection validation below records the stricter solution now obtained for this first-event case, without claiming universal convergence. Remaining-time handling is verified analytically only; no general repeated-contact loop, nonpenetration repair, native driving collision response or original-game comparison is claimed. Raw game data and reports remain local.

Normal projection validation

The normal-projection milestone added two ordinary CPU fixtures (262 total at that stage); eleven explicit offscreen GPU and six window tests retain separate scope. One fixture solves three distinct clustered friction contacts at spacings 0.01, 0.001, 0.0005 and 0.0001 m using 1e-7 m/s tolerance, checks all points remain reported, normal nonpenetration, friction cones, energy loss, fixed pose and reversed contact order. The other constructs a four-contact normal response matrix independently through public unit point impulses, enumerates all 16 active subsets with pivoted Gaussian elimination, checks complementarity and compares final chassis velocity, rotation rate and energy to the projected result. The existing 64-duplicate, covariance, moving-rack work and rollback fixtures still pass. The nonconvergence fixture now uses asymmetric contact points, since the former symmetric case can converge in one projected sweep.

The application first-event fixture now retains friction 0.3 at 1e-7 m/s tolerance, replacing its earlier zero-friction isolation. Local BMW/Drift wall-step examples/wall-step.json also uses 1e-7 m/s. The projected path converges in 13 sweeps with residual 3.948609e-8 m/s; impact work is -2432.755045 J and post-impact energy 4956.873632 J. Energy-balance residual is -1.364e-12 J. The source event time/pose remain those of the retained midpoint proposal; only the impact solution is refined. An independent per-contact/momentum/work audit verifies the strict result.

The separate deeply overlapping static wall-impact example retains 1e-4 m/s. Its sequential path still converges in 533 sweeps with residual 9.996162e-5 m/s and unchanged energy/work relative to the previous result. The projected path alone does not solve every manifold, and the stricter static case still has no established convergence within the configured budget. This record does not imply a complete repeated-contact driving loop or original-game collision fidelity. Original game data and research outputs remain local.

Certified departure validation

Five additional ordinary fixtures bring the Rust total to 267; eleven explicit offscreen GPU and six window tests keep separate scope. Three ground fixtures cover analytical interior rotation extrema, an offset box centre, 24 translated/rotated motions against 1001 independently evaluated poses and all eight vertices, invalid axes, stationary/tangential/outward proximity paths, inward crossing, initial penetration and a rotation that intersects despite clear endpoints. World covariance is checked at a translated reference of order 1e5 m. A second wall fixture ensures that certifying an initial departure cannot hide a later obstacle. The session fixture consumes a force-free post-impact remainder and confirms renewed inward force still returns a zero-time event. The CLI fixture verifies opt-in/default behavior and positive retained certificates without changing earlier query semantics.

The local BMW/Drift wall-sweep examples/wall-sweep.json now contains a retreat from AC_PIT_0-relative [-5.462312928183368,-0.04,0] to [-4.5,-0.04,0] m. It has six candidates, eleven evaluations, no event and two certified triangles (retained indices 1281 and 1283). Their minimum projected-gap bounds are 9.9999484e-7 m. An independent raw-geometry world-space audit evaluates 1001 poses and all collider vertices per certificate, obtaining a minimum 9.9999998e-7 m, above both conservative bounds. The earlier three paths retain their previous fractions/classification; all four paths (4004 sampled poses) agree with the independent SAT audit. Sampling corroborates these traces; the extrema calculation supplies the whole-path bound. Source data and generated reports remain local.

A certificate requires positive separation, including its f64 allowance. Exact contact, initial overlap and renewed inward motion remain deliberately unresolved by this mechanism. These checks do not establish a complete persistent/resting-contact force law, continuous native gameplay collision response or original-game parity.
